This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. We're learning more about the people
who confronted a gunman during an elementary school shooting in Oregon yesterday. Police say
their actions likely prevented further violence after three children and a teacher were killed.
Oregon Public Broadcasting's Bryce Doyle reports. The gunman was a 16-year-old former student.
Police say he jumped a fence with a shotgun and a backpack full of ammo. He shot at a person in a
pickup truck after the driver confronted him, then blasted his way through the school's locked doors.
The gunman then opened fire in a special education classroom. Ben Police chief Mike Krantz described
what happened next. A teacher in the classroom threw her cell phone at the suspect and then tackled
him and fought to take the firearm from him. She was not injured in that incident, but she almost
certainly helped prevent more bloodshed. A parent who had seen the shooting outside the school
followed the gunman inside and shot him multiple times with a handgun, killing him. Two other
people were shot, a seven-year-old student and a 54-year-old teacher. They're receiving care at
regional hospitals. For NPR News, I'm Bryce Dole. White House Press Secretary Katie Zachariya is
out after just five days on the job. NPR's Emily Fang reports questions emerged about how Zachariya
presented her legal credentials. Trump has referred to her as an attorney and Zachariya did go to law
school, but there is no record of her passing the bar in any state. And when she was asked about
this, she responded that she had passed when she moved to China. I've lived in China for the better
part of a decade. It is just not possible for foreigners to take the bar there or even practice
law. NPR's Emily Fang reporting, "Russian attacks knocked out power to hundreds of thousands of
Ukrainian households and wounded at least 15 people. The bombardment before cold weather arrives
has been an annual feature of the nearly five-year-old war, and the strikes come amid fears that
deteriorating relations between Ukraine and the U.S. could leave Ukraine further exposed this winter.
Evacuations are underway in Southern California from a fast-moving brush fire near San Clemente.
NPR's Nate Rott reports at least four homes appear to be affected.
It's these hot, dry Santa Ana winds that have been scouring much of Southern California all
day, prompting power outages and fueling a handful of wildfires that have sparked up.
The Norte fire near San Clemente is currently the most active. The Orange County Fire Authority
says at least four homes have been impacted and the fire continues to grow. It's urging people
to stay away from the area. Hot temperatures and strong winds are forecast to continue through
most of Saturday. Nate Rott, NPR News. The Coast Guard says it has rescued at least 16 people
floating in the Pacific Ocean following a May Day call from a sinking vessel off of Mexico's Baja
California coast. Another 11 people are believed to be missing. One of those rescued was being
treated for a suspected shark bite. It's in an area frequented by smugglers transporting migrants,
but also popular with fishing and leisure boats. You're listening to NPR News from Washington.
A New Mexico judge has dismissed a grand jury indictment that accused actor Timothy
Busfield of four counts of criminal sexual contact with a child. The judge cited prosecutorial
misconduct and errors that undermined the grand jury process. Busfield denied the allegations,
describing them as a vendetta pursued by the parents of two boys who were let go from a show
he was directing. People with a certain gene variant have a higher risk of developing Alzheimer's
disease. NPR's Ping Huang reports it may have to do with how their brain cells respond to stress.
The APOE gene helps transport lipids, which are tiny globules of fat, through the brain.
Many Alzheimer's patients have a variant called APOE4, which seems to cause malfunction in some
people's brain cells. Lipids accumulate as droplets instead of forming a protective sheath
around the cell's axons. Researchers at MIT have started to figure out how that happens.
Layla Akai, lead author on a new study, says it's typically a stress response.
This can happen in response to too many nutrients, to having not enough nutrients,
to thermal cues, other kinds of stressful cues. Akai and her colleagues conducted
experiments on lab-grown human brain cells and mice. They found that manipulating a key
enzyme could reverse the damage, offering a potential target for future Alzheimer's treatments.
The paper is published in the journal Cell Stem Cell, Ping Huang, NPR News.
Leaf peeping season is underway. According to the Foliage Report website, New England is having an
elite year thanks to adequate spring and summer rain, plus warm days and cool nights heading into
fall. Colorado, meanwhile, is having a lackluster foliage season because of extreme droughts.
I'm Rylan Barton. This is NPR.
